title: Peter On The Ledge
subject: Torts
stem:
In preparation for a Bible-study group’s mountain-climbing weekend, Daniel purchased the necessary climbing equipment from Lydia’s Outdoor Goods, a retail dealer in sporting goods. A week later, Daniel fell from a rock face when a safety device he had purchased from Lydia’s Outdoor Goods malfunctioned because of a defect in its manufacture. Peter was severely injured when he tried to reach and assist Daniel on the ledge to which Daniel had fallen. Peter’s injury was not caused by any fault on his own part.

If Peter brings an action against Lydia’s Outdoor Goods to recover damages for his injuries, will Peter prevail?

Source row: BARMATRIX Q#15257 gives the original Torts / Strict Liability and Products Liability question, answer choices, official key D, and official explanation that the rescuer can recover because injury to a person in the rescuer’s position was foreseeable if the safety device failed.
call: If Peter brings an action against Lydia’s Outdoor Goods to recover damages for his injuries, will Peter prevail?

choices.A: No, because Lydia’s Outdoor Goods could not have discovered the defect by a reasonable inspection of the safety device.
choices.B: No, because Peter did not rely on the representation of safety implied from the sale of the safety device by Lydia’s Outdoor Goods.
choices.C: Yes, because Daniel was not negligent in failing to test the safety device.
choices.D: Yes, because injury to a person in Peter’s position was foreseeable if the safety device failed.

rightExplanation: D is correct. Peter is the injured rescuer. The defect in the safety device caused Daniel to fall, and a rescue attempt is a foreseeable response to a climber stranded on a ledge. Gold Key: In a defective-product case, do not stop at the buyer/user. A commercial seller can be liable for physical harm to a foreseeable non-user, including a rescuer, when the product defect creates the danger that leads to the rescue. Silver Key: Lock the plaintiff in the call. Peter, not Daniel, is suing; the answer must explain why Peter’s injury is within the product-risk chain.

wrongExplanations.A: This answer uses a negligence-style inspection frame. It focuses on whether Lydia’s Outdoor Goods could have discovered the manufacturing defect. That is not the product-liability path this question is testing. Gold Key: Retailer inspection is not the gate in a strict products-liability claim; the key is defective product + commercial seller + harm within the risk.
wrongExplanations.B: This answer uses a reliance / representation frame. Peter does not need to be the buyer or to rely on an implied representation of safety if his injury is a foreseeable result of the defective product. Gold Key: Foreseeable non-users and rescuers are not cut out merely because they did not buy or rely on the product.
wrongExplanations.C: This answer reaches the correct result but for the wrong reason. Daniel’s lack of negligence in failing to test the device is not the reason Peter recovers from the retailer. Silver Key: When the call is Peter v. retailer, cut answers that make Daniel’s conduct the deciding reason unless the stem makes Daniel’s conduct the legal gate.

c3.label: CUT A — wrong frame
c3.text: A talks about whether the retailer could discover the defect. That is the inspection / negligence frame. The call asks whether Peter, the rescuer, can recover for injury caused by the product failure. Cut as bait_doctrine, NOT_RESPONSIVE, anchor-assisted.

c3.label: CUT B — wrong frame
c3.text: B talks about Peter’s reliance on an implied representation. That is a buyer / warranty / reliance frame. Peter’s claim is not defeated merely because he did not rely on the sale. Cut as bait_doctrine, NOT_RESPONSIVE, anchor-assisted.

c3.label: CUT C — wrong element
c3.text: C gives the right “yes” outcome but points to Daniel’s conduct. The call is Peter v. Lydia’s Outdoor Goods. Daniel’s failure to test is not the reason Peter recovers. Cut as wrong_element, NOT_RESPONSIVE, hard structural.

c3.label: Residual D
c3.text: D is the only answer that names Peter’s position and connects the injury to the safety device’s failure. It is true and responsive.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: Not needed after the anchor-assisted cut.

studentScript: Peter sues. Device failed. Rescue injury followed. Cut inspection, cut reliance, cut Daniel’s conduct. Pick the answer that ties Peter’s injury to foreseeable product failure: D.

A.signal: The answer discusses retailer inspection rather than Peter’s product-caused rescue injury.
A.lawyer: In strict products liability, a commercial seller’s reasonable care or inability to discover a manufacturing defect does not defeat liability when the defect causes covered harm.

B.signal: The answer asks whether Peter relied on the sale rather than whether Peter’s injury was a foreseeable product-risk injury.
B.lawyer: A foreseeable injured rescuer or non-user is not barred merely because he did not buy or rely on the product.

C.signal: The answer says yes, but its reason is Daniel’s conduct. The call asks why Peter recovers from Lydia’s Outdoor Goods.
C.lawyer: Daniel’s possible negligence is not the affirmative reason Peter recovers. The product defect and foreseeable rescue injury supply the liability path.

D.signal: This answer names Peter’s position and ties the injury to the safety device’s failure.
D.lawyer: A rescuer injured in a foreseeable rescue attempt after a defective safety device fails is within the scope of product-caused harm.

goldKeys.statement: In a defective-product case, a commercial seller’s inspection care and the rescuer’s reliance are not the gate; a foreseeable non-user or rescuer can recover when the defect creates the danger that leads to the injury.
goldKeys.trigger: defective safety product injures a rescuer who responds to the danger
goldKeys.unlocks: inspection/reliance traps and the non-user rescuer trap
goldKeys.authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability § 1; Vandermark v. Ford Motor Co.; Wagner v. International Railway Co.

silverKeys.statement: Lock the plaintiff in the call. When the rescuer sues the retailer, downgrade answers about the buyer’s conduct, the seller’s inspection, or reliance unless they decide the rescuer’s claim.
silverKeys.trigger: call names the rescuer as plaintiff
silverKeys.unlocks: rescuer-v-retailer call versus adjacent Daniel/inspection/reliance traps

remediation.title: The rescuer is the plaintiff
remediation.signal: defective product imperils one person; rescuer is injured
remediation.studentMove: Ask whether the answer explains the rescuer’s claim against the seller.
remediation.tinyRule: Do not let inspection, reliance, or the user’s conduct replace the plaintiff in the call.
remediation.trap: Students answer Daniel’s or Lydia’s adjacent issue instead of Peter’s claim.
